The Pygmy rabbit (Sylvilagus idahoensis) is one of the smallest leporids in North America, and its life-history traits reflect the constrained energetic limits typical of a small-bodied herbivore inhabiting semi-arid sagebrush steppe. Basal metabolic rate, measured via respirometry trials on captive individuals at a core body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], averages approximately 384.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = approximately 384.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value consistent with allometric predictions for a mammal with an adult body mass of about 432 grams. This modest metabolic expenditure under standard resting conditions is closely tied to the species' reliance on a low-quality, fibrous diet dominated by Artemisia tridentata, which imposes significant digestive constraints. The relatively low basal expenditure helps offset the high costs of thermoregulation in the cold, arid environments the species occupies across the Intermountain West. Field and laboratory studies alike confirm that the species operates on a tight energetic margin, with daily energy requirements barely exceeding basal needs during winter months. Such physiological conservation has direct implications for growth, reproduction, and overall life-history scheduling, setting the stage for a suite of developmental and reproductive parameters that are finely tuned to seasonal resource pulses.

Reproductive output in Sylvilagus idahoensis is moderate relative to other small lagomorphs, shaped by both the brevity of the active season and the energetic demands of lactation. Females typically produce three litters per year [F_R_i = three litters per year], with each litter containing an average of six pups [N_R_i = each litter containing an average of six pups]. These values, recorded in wild populations at a maternal body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], indicate a maximum annual reproductive rate that, while not exceptional among rabbits, allows for population persistence under the unpredictable precipitation regimes of sagebrush ecosystems. The timing of litters is tightly synchronized with the spring green-up of perennial forbs, which provide the high-quality forage necessary for milk production. Pups are born in a relatively altricial state, and the rapid succession of litters means that females must sustain high metabolic throughput through much of the growing season. Litter size and frequency together represent a balanced trade-off between current reproductive investment and the need for maternal survival into subsequent years, a common pattern among small mammals occupying resource-limited habitats.

Neonatal body mass in the Pygmy rabbit is modest, reflecting the species' small adult size and the energetic constraints of gestation. Newborns weigh approximately 15.7 grams [Wwb = approximately 15.7 grams] at parturition, a value comparable to that of other small Sylvilagus species when scaled to maternal body mass. This initial wet weight is derived from allometric relationships within the genus, where a 450-gram adult female (450 grams) [Wwi = 450 grams] produces neonates that are roughly 3.5 percent of her own mass. The relatively small offspring size is typical of altricial mammals and is associated with a short gestational period that minimizes the cumulative energetic burden on the mother. At the other end of the developmental spectrum, the ultimate adult body mass, reached after the completion of skeletal growth, generally falls between 375 and 500 grams, with the 450-gram value (450 grams) [Wwi = 450 grams] representing a frequently cited asymptotic mass for well-nourished individuals. This modest adult size likely confers advantages in terms of reduced absolute food requirements and the ability to exploit thermal refugia within dense sagebrush canopies, though it also limits the capacity for extended fasting during harsh winter conditions.

The developmental trajectory from birth to independence is compressed into a relatively brief window, consistent with the species' strategy of multiple litters per year. At a maternal body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], weaning occurs at approximately 13 days after birth [tx = approximately 13 days after birth], a remarkably short nursing period that places considerable demands on the quality of maternal milk. By this stage, the young have tripled their birth mass to reach a wet weight at weaning of approximately 46.4 grams [Wwx = approximately 46.4 grams], reflecting the rapid growth rates that are characteristic of leporids. This swift transition to independent feeding is essential for allowing females to quickly redirect energy toward the next litter in the sequence. Gestation itself is also brief, lasting about 28 days [tg = about 28 days] at 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], consistent with the range of 27 to 30 days reported for several other Sylvilagus species. The short gestation and early weaning together epitomize a life-history strategy that prioritizes high annual fecundity over extended maternal investment in any single litter, an adaptive response to the high juvenile predation rates and unpredictable resource availability that characterize sagebrush steppe habitats.

Sexual maturation in the Pygmy rabbit occurs relatively late for a mammal of its body size, reflecting a life-history trade-off between early reproduction and the need to achieve sufficient body mass to survive winter and compete for breeding territories. The time since birth at puberty is approximately 256 days [tp = approximately 256 days], meaning that individuals born in the spring typically do not reach reproductive maturity until the following breeding season. This delay ensures that first-time breeders have completed skeletal growth and accumulated sufficient fat reserves before undertaking the energetic costs of gestation and lactation. In terms of overall longevity, the maximum lifespan in the wild is estimated at 11.5 years [am = 11.5 years] under average thermal conditions of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], a remarkably long duration for a leporid of its size and one that suggests low extrinsic mortality in the absence of heavy predation pressure. This extended lifespan, combined with delayed puberty and moderate annual reproductive output, positions the Pygmy rabbit as a relatively slow-paced strategist within the fast-lived Lagomorpha lineage.
